en.title: Access to internal portals
en.summary: Bookmarks, an internet shortcut, a note on the reset of single sign-on and a password export that lead to internal portals. Opening an address raises an event.
en.guide:
# Access to internal portals

Users and administrators note the addresses of internal portals in bookmarks, shortcuts, notes and exports. The files below hold such addresses. The files share the honeytokens of the story, so the same address appears in every file that names the same portal. Nothing stands behind the addresses: the accounts and passwords exist nowhere. You decide which files you place and where; one is enough, and they need not lie together.

## Browser bookmarks

The file `bookmarks.html` is an export of browser bookmarks in the format that every common browser writes and imports. In the bookmarks bar, a folder `Example Ltd` holds the link `VPN self-service`, which leads to `Honeytoken-URL-Portal`. That URL belongs to a URL honeytoken: following the link raises an event and redirects the browser to the redirect target of the honeytoken.

### Placing the file

1. Give the honeytoken a redirect target that fits the name of the portal, such as the public login page of a service that you use.
2. Either place the file as an export, for example in the documents of an account that exists only for this purpose or in a backup of a user profile, or import it into the browser of such an account, so that the link appears in its bookmarks.
3. Add bookmarks of your own around it, such as the public sites of your organization, so that the file does not hold a single folder.
4. Record where you placed it in the notes of the scenario.

### Testing

Open the file in a browser and follow the link, or import it and open the bookmark. Within a minute, the scenario shows an incident. Close the incident after the test.

## Note on the reset of single sign-on

The file `SSO-reset.html` is a short note of the IT department of `Example Ltd` with a link to a portal for resetting the single sign-on: `Honeytoken-URL-Portal`. The URL belongs to a URL honeytoken: whoever follows the link raises an event and is redirected to the redirect target of the honeytoken.

### Placing the file

1. Give the honeytoken a redirect target that fits the portal, such as the public login page of a service that you use.
2. Place the file where an intruder looks for ways to take over accounts: on a file share of the IT department, in a folder with notes for the service desk, in the documents of an account that exists only for this purpose.
3. Change `Contact` to a team that exists.
4. Record where you placed it in the notes of the scenario.

### Testing

Open the file in a browser on a computer with access to the internet and follow the link. Within a minute, the scenario shows an incident. Close the incident after the test.

## Internet shortcut

The file `Portal.url` is a Windows shortcut to the URL `Honeytoken-URL-Link`. That URL belongs to a URL honeytoken: opening the shortcut opens it in the browser, which raises an event, and the browser is redirected to the redirect target of the honeytoken, or to the default target of the trigger.

### Placing the file

1. Give the honeytoken a redirect target that fits the name of the shortcut, such as the public login page of a service that you use. Whoever opens the shortcut sees that page.
2. Rename the file so that its name promises something valuable, such as `VPN access.url`, `Payroll.url` or `Admin console.url`. The extension `.url` must stay.
3. Place it where an intruder looks around, such as the desktop or the documents of an account that exists only for this purpose, a file share of the IT department or a folder with handover notes.
4. Record where you placed it in the notes of the scenario.

### Testing

Open the shortcut on a computer with access to the internet. Within a minute, the scenario shows an incident. Close the incident after the test.

## Password export of a browser

The file `Passwords.csv` has the columns that Chrome, Edge and other browsers write when the user exports saved passwords. Three entries belong to the account `j.doe`; the address of one of them is `Honeytoken-URL-Portal`. That URL belongs to a URL honeytoken: whoever opens the address, for example to try the password, raises an event and is redirected to the redirect target of the honeytoken. The passwords exist nowhere.

### Placing the file

1. Give the honeytoken a redirect target that fits the entry, such as the public login page of a service that you use.
2. Place the file where a user leaves an export that they should have deleted: in the downloads or documents of an account that exists only for this purpose, or on a share of the IT department.
3. Rename the entries if your own naming scheme differs from `wiki`, `build` and `portal`.
4. Record where you placed it in the notes of the scenario.

### Testing

Open the URL of the third entry in a browser on a computer with access to the internet. Within a minute, the scenario shows an incident. Close the incident after the test.

## Pocket litter

The files `Meeting-notes.md` and `Favorites.html` hold no honeytoken and raise no event, whatever happens to them. They give the story a believable surrounding: place them in the same places as the other files of the story, beside the files that raise an event.

## Limits

- Whoever reads one of the files, or looks at the properties of the shortcut, sees the URL. It names the address of your trigger and a random value.
- `bookmarks.html`: Opening the file shows the bookmarks; only following the link raises an event.
- `SSO-reset.html`: Opening the file raises no event; only following the link does.
- `Portal.url`: The shortcut raises an event only when someone opens it. Windows Explorer does not request the URL when it lists the folder.
- `Passwords.csv`: Only someone who opens the address raises an event. Reading the file does not.
- `Passwords.csv`: The first two entries point to names under `corp.example.com` that you do not control through Nyktus. Make sure that nobody enters these passwords anywhere, or that those names do not exist in your network.

en.title: PostgreSQL objects that travel with every backup
en.summary: SQL for two objects of your PostgreSQL database. A restore of a dump on another machine resolves the name of a DNS honeytoken, and so does a query of the second object.
en.guide:
# PostgreSQL objects that travel with every backup

The deception attaches the trigger to your backup itself. An intruder who steals a dump of your database restores it on a machine of their own, where a restore script that only points at your host would never run. Both files are SQL for your database, with the DNS honeytoken host `Honeytoken-Domain`. You run them once; every dump you take afterwards carries the objects. Neither file creates a table with data, and neither changes data.

## The object that fires on restore

`restore-hook.sql` creates the function `refresh_catalog_stats` and the materialized view `catalog_stats`, which calls it. A dump holds the view without its contents and refreshes it when it is restored, in the custom and the directory format as well as in a plain dump. The refresh calls the function, and its connection attempt with `dblink` resolves the host name, which raises an event. Creating the view in your own database runs the function once, so the file tests itself.

1. Check that the extension `dblink` is available: it ships with PostgreSQL in the package `postgresql-contrib` or with the server itself, depending on the distribution. The function names `public.dblink_connect`, because a restore runs with an empty search path.
2. Run the file in your database: `psql -d DATABASE -f restore-hook.sql`. The role needs the right to create an extension and objects in the schema `public`.
3. Choose `FunctionName` and `ViewName` when you apply the deception, so that they fit your schema. Both appear in the dump.

## The object that fires on a query

`foreign-table.sql` creates a foreign table `customer_payment_tokens` that points to a remote database. It is part of the schema, survives every dump format and resolves the host name only when someone queries the table, for example while searching for tables with valuable names.

1. Check that the extension `postgres_fdw` is available.
2. Run the file in your database. Choose a name for the table that an intruder wants to read.

## Testing

Take a dump with `pg_dump DATABASE > dump.sql` and restore it into an empty database on a computer with access to the internet: `psql -d TEST -f dump.sql`. Within a minute, the scenario shows an incident. Then query the foreign table with `SELECT * FROM customer_payment_tokens` for a second one. Close the incidents after the test. Use one deception for each database or backup set, so that an incident tells you which data was stolen. Tell your database administrators: a test restore on a machine with internet access raises an event as well.

## Limits

- A restore in a network that cannot resolve names on the internet does not reach the DNS role. That holds for every beacon in a backup: it catches the intruder who restores your backup on a machine of their own, not one who works in an isolated laboratory.
- Whoever searches the dump for host names, or looks at the objects of the restored database, can find the name unusual.
- The restore needs the extension `dblink` on the machine of the intruder. Without it the dump reports an error for the extension and the function does not run.

en.title: QR code labels in the server room
en.summary: Three printed QR codes for a rack, a device and a patch panel. Whoever scans one raises an event, which shows that somebody stands in the room with a phone.
en.guide:
# QR code labels in the server room

This deception has no file to download: it gives you three URLs, which you print as QR codes and attach to equipment, as asset labels often are. Whoever scans a code opens the URL in the browser of their phone, which raises an event and redirects the browser to the redirect target of the honeytoken. The event shows the address of the phone, often a mobile network or the guest network, and a mobile browser. In a server room, both are unusual.

- Rack: `Honeytoken-URL-Rack`
- Device: `Honeytoken-URL-Device`
- Patch panel: `Honeytoken-URL-PatchPanel`

## Placing the labels

1. Open each honeytoken in the console. It shows the QR code of its URL, which you can print. Print each code on a label with a caption that fits where it goes, as the asset labels in your room look: for the rack, the asset number and the text "Documentation"; for the device, "Service and warranty"; for the patch panel, "Port plan".
2. Attach the labels where an intruder in the room looks: the frame or inside of the door of the rack for the first, the inside of the cover of a device or a drive tray for the second, the front of the patch panel or the door of the network cabinet for the third.
3. Attach them in addition to your real labels, not instead of them.
4. Give each honeytoken a redirect target that fits its caption, such as the public page of the manufacturer or of your organization. Whoever scans the code then sees a page and does not notice a trap.
5. Use a honeytoken of its own for each rack, device or cabinet. The incident then tells you where the person stood. Record where you attached each label in the placement notes of the honeytoken.
6. Tell the people who work in the room. Whoever scans a label out of curiosity raises an event as well.

## Testing

Scan each code with a phone. Within a minute, the scenario shows an incident. Close the incidents after the test.

## Limits

- An event happens only when somebody scans the code. A person who only looks at the label, or photographs it, raises none.
- The URL shows the address of your trigger and a random value. Whoever reads the code with a scanner that shows the address sees it.
- A phone that scans over a VPN of the organization shows its address, not a mobile network.

en.title: Registry export with backup settings

The server name belongs to a DNS honeytoken: whoever uses the settings to reach the server resolves the name, which raises an event. There is no server behind it, and the account and password exist nowhere.

## Placing the file

1. Place the file where an intruder looks for settings of backup software: on a server that is backed up, in a folder with documentation of the IT department, in a backup of a user profile.
2. Rename it after the software if you use another one, and change `Vendor` when you apply the deception, so that the key fits.
3. Do not import the file on a computer that you use. It writes the key to the registry of the account that imports it.
4. Record where you placed it in the notes of the scenario.

## Testing

Resolve the name with `nslookup Honeytoken-Domain` on a computer with access to the internet. Within a minute, the scenario shows an incident. Close the incident after the test.

## Limits

- Only a lookup that reaches the DNS role of Nyktus raises an event. A network without name resolution to the internet, or a resolver that answers from its cache, prevents it.
- The server name is a random label under the zone of your DNS role. An intruder who reads the file carefully can find it unusual.
- Importing the file creates the key but starts nothing, so an intruder who only imports it does not raise an event. The lookup happens when something connects to the server.

en.title: Remote access of administrators
en.summary: Connections of administrators to servers: Remote Desktop, SSH, an Ansible inventory and a WireGuard tunnel. Connecting resolves the name of a DNS honeytoken.
en.guide:
# Remote access of administrators

Administrators reach servers over Remote Desktop, SSH, an Ansible inventory and a VPN tunnel. The files below hold these connections. The files share the honeytokens of the story, so the same host name appears in every file that names the same service. Nothing stands behind the names: the accounts, tokens and passwords exist nowhere. You decide which files you place and where; one is enough, and they need not lie together.

## Remote Desktop connection

The file `Server.rdp` is a saved connection of the Remote Desktop client of Windows to the server `Honeytoken-Domain-Server`, with the account `adm.jdoe@corp.example.com`. The server name belongs to a DNS honeytoken: before the client connects, it resolves the name, which raises an event. There is no server behind it, so the connection fails.

### Placing the file

1. Place the file where an intruder looks for access to further systems, such as the desktop or the documents of an administrative account that exists only for this purpose, a jump server, or a file share of the IT department.
2. Rename it after a server that the intruder would want to reach, such as `Backup server.rdp` or `Domain controller.rdp`. The extension `.rdp` must stay.
3. Record where you placed it in the notes of the scenario.

### Testing

Open the file on a Windows computer with access to the internet and click "Connect". Within a minute, the scenario shows an incident. Close the incident after the test.

## SSH configuration with a jump host

The file `config` is an SSH client configuration. It sends every connection to a host under `corp.example.com`, and every connection to `jump`, through the jump host `Honeytoken-Domain-JumpHost`. That name belongs to a DNS honeytoken: before SSH connects, it resolves the name, and the lookup raises an event. The connection itself fails, because the name has no SSH server behind it.

### Placing the file

1. Place the file where an intruder looks for access to further hosts, for example as `~/.ssh/config` of an account on a jump server or an administration workstation, or on a file share among scripts and notes of the IT department.
2. On a system where the file is used as `~/.ssh/config`, restrict it to its owner: `chmod 600 ~/.ssh/config`. SSH refuses configuration files that others can write to.
3. Do not place it where colleagues use it for their own work. Every legitimate `ssh` to a host under `corp.example.com` would raise an event.
4. Record where you placed it in the notes of the scenario, so that it can be found again and removed.

### Testing

Run `ssh -F config jump` on a computer that resolves names through the internet. Within a minute, the scenario shows an incident. Close the incident after the test.

## Ansible inventory

The file `inventory.ini` is an Ansible inventory with the groups `web` and `app`. The group `app` holds the host `Honeytoken-Domain-Application`. The name belongs to a DNS honeytoken: a playbook that runs against all hosts, or an SSH connection to that host, resolves it, which raises an event. There is no server behind it. The hosts of the group `web` are names under `corp.example.com` that you do not create; make sure that they do not exist in your network, or change them to hosts that do and are not managed by Ansible.

### Placing the file

1. Place the file where an intruder looks for the servers of an application: in a repository of automation, on an administration server, in a backup of such a repository.
2. Do not place it where you run Ansible. A run against all hosts would resolve the name and raise an event.
3. Record where you placed it in the notes of the scenario.

### Testing

Run `ansible -i inventory.ini app -m ping` on a computer with Ansible and access to the internet. The command fails after the lookup. Within a minute, the scenario shows an incident. Close the incident after the test.

## WireGuard configuration for a tunnel

The file `wg0.conf` is the client configuration of a WireGuard tunnel to the gateway `Honeytoken-Domain-Gateway`. The keys are random values in the form of WireGuard keys. The name of the gateway belongs to a DNS honeytoken: whoever brings up the tunnel with `wg-quick up` or imports the file into a WireGuard client resolves the name, which raises an event. There is no gateway behind it, and the keys exist nowhere.

### Placing the file

1. Place the file where an intruder looks for access to the network: in the home directory of an administrator account that exists only for this purpose, in a folder with VPN profiles on a file share of the IT department, or in a backup of a workstation.
2. Rename it if the place calls for another name, such as `office.conf`. The extension `.conf` must stay.
3. Do not copy it to `/etc/wireguard`: a system service would bring the tunnel up on every start and raise events.
4. Record where you placed it in the notes of the scenario.

### Testing

Run `nslookup Honeytoken-Domain-Gateway` on a computer with access to the internet; `sudo wg-quick up ./wg0.conf` on a computer with WireGuard has the same effect. Within a minute, the scenario shows an incident. Close the incident after the test.

## Pocket litter

The files `shell-history.txt` and `Tickets.csv` hold no honeytoken and raise no event, whatever happens to them. They give the story a believable surrounding: place them in the same places as the other files of the story, beside the files that raise an event.

## Limits

- Only a lookup that reaches the DNS role of Nyktus raises an event. A network without name resolution to the internet, or a resolver that answers from its cache, prevents it.
- The host names are random labels under the zone of your DNS role. An intruder who reads the files carefully can find them unusual.
- `wg0.conf`: WireGuard resolves the endpoint when the tunnel comes up. An intruder who only reads the file does not raise an event.

en.title: Shell history with commands for servers
en.summary: The history files of a Linux shell and of PowerShell, with a command that logs in to a database and commands that open a remote session. Running them resolves the name of a DNS honeytoken.
en.guide:
# Shell history with commands for servers

Administrators and developers leave the commands they typed in the history of their shell, passwords and host names included. The files below tell this story for Linux and for Windows. The files do not share a honeytoken: the database and the server have names of their own. Nothing stands behind the names, and the accounts and passwords exist nowhere. You decide which file you place and where; one is enough.

## History of a Linux shell

The file `bash_history` is the history of a Linux shell. It holds the command that logs in to the database `billing` on `Honeytoken-Domain-Database` with the account `svc-ops` and a random password. The host name belongs to a DNS honeytoken: whoever runs the command, or anything else that connects to the host, resolves it, which raises an event. No database stands behind it, and the account and password exist nowhere.

### Placing the file

1. Name the file `.bash_history` and place it in the home directory of an account on an application server that people log in to.
2. If the account has a history already, append the lines to it instead of replacing it: a history that is new, and has nothing older than the lures, looks made.
3. Record where you placed it in the notes of the scenario.

### Testing

Resolve the host with `nslookup Honeytoken-Domain-Database` on a computer with access to the internet. Within a minute, the scenario shows an incident. Close the incident after the test.

## History of PowerShell

The file `ConsoleHost_history.txt` is the PSReadLine history of PowerShell. It holds the commands that ask for the credentials of the account `CORP\svc-ops` and open a remote session to `Honeytoken-Domain-Server`. The host name belongs to a DNS honeytoken: whoever runs the commands, or anything else that connects to the server, resolves it, which raises an event. No server stands behind it, and the account exists nowhere. The file holds no password: PowerShell does not write command lines with passwords to its history.

### Placing the file

1. Place the file as `ConsoleHost_history.txt` in the directory `%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine` of an account on a server or workstation of administrators.
2. If the account has a history already, append the lines to it instead of replacing it.
3. Record where you placed it in the notes of the scenario.

### Testing

Resolve the host with `nslookup Honeytoken-Domain-Server` on a computer with access to the internet. Within a minute, the scenario shows an incident. Close the incident after the test.

## Limits

- Only a lookup that reaches the DNS role of Nyktus raises an event. A network without name resolution to the internet, or a resolver that answers from its cache, prevents it.
- The host names are random labels under the zone of your DNS role. An intruder who reads the files carefully can find them unusual.
- Reading the files raises no event; using the credentials or running the commands does.
- `ConsoleHost_history.txt`: PSReadLine does not write command lines with a password, token or secret to the history, so a PowerShell history with a password would be unusual. The file therefore holds the account and the server but no password.

files.content:

ls -la
mysql -h Honeytoken-Domain-Database -u svc-ops -pKrnaqEUeIaHCav1S4RWy billing
sudo systemctl restart nginx
tail -n 50 /var/log/nginx/error.log
exit

Enter-PSSession -ComputerName Honeytoken-Domain-Server -Credential $cred
Get-EventLog -LogName System -Newest 20
exit

en.title: Access to virtualization and backup
en.summary: A PowerShell profile for vCenter and notes on the backup repository, with accounts and passwords. Connecting resolves the name of a DNS honeytoken.
en.guide:
# Access to virtualization and backup

The access to the virtualization platform and to the backup repository is among the most valuable that an intruder can find, because whoever holds it can read or delete the machines and their backups. The files below hold it. The files share the honeytokens of the story, so the same host name appears in every file that names the same service. Nothing stands behind the names: the accounts, tokens and passwords exist nowhere. You decide which files you place and where; one is enough, and they need not lie together.

## PowerShell profile for vCenter

The file `Connect-VCenter.ps1` connects to the vCenter server `Honeytoken-Domain-VCenter` with the account `svc-vmops@vsphere.local` and lists the virtual machines. The name of the server belongs to a DNS honeytoken: whoever runs the script, or connects to the server with the credentials, resolves it, which raises an event. There is no server behind it, so the connection fails, and the account and password exist nowhere. The script only reads and sends nothing from the computer on which it runs.

### Placing the file

1. Place the file where an intruder looks for access to the virtualization: on an administration server, on a file share of the IT department, in a folder with scripts in the profile of an account that exists only for this purpose.
2. Do not place it where a scheduled task or a colleague runs it.
3. Record where you placed it in the notes of the scenario.

### Testing

Run `nslookup Honeytoken-Domain-VCenter` on a computer with access to the internet; running the script with VMware PowerCLI has the same effect. Within a minute, the scenario shows an incident. Close the incident after the test.

## Notes on the backup repository

The file `Backup-repository.txt` is a note of an administrator about the repository of the backups. It names the share `\\Honeytoken-Domain-Repository\Repository` and the account `CORP\svc-vmops` with a random password. The server name belongs to a DNS honeytoken: whoever opens the share resolves it, which raises an event. There is no server behind it, and the account and password exist nowhere. Intruders who prepare ransomware look for exactly this.

### Placing the file

1. Place the file where an intruder looks for the backups: on the backup server, on an administration server, on a file share of the IT department.
2. Change `Contact` to a team that exists.
3. Record where you placed it in the notes of the scenario.

### Testing

Open `\\Honeytoken-Domain-Repository\Repository` in the Windows Explorer of a computer with access to the internet, or resolve the name with `nslookup Honeytoken-Domain-Repository`. Within a minute, the scenario shows an incident. Close the incident after the test.

## Limits

- Only a lookup that reaches the DNS role of Nyktus raises an event. A network without name resolution to the internet, or a resolver that answers from its cache, prevents it.
- The host names are random labels under the zone of your DNS role. An intruder who reads the files carefully can find them unusual.
- `Connect-VCenter.ps1`: The script needs VMware PowerCLI. Where it is missing, running the script fails before the lookup.

$credential = New-Object System.Management.Automation.PSCredential($user, $password)

en.title: Script that detects a copy of your website
en.summary: A small script for your own website. Served from another host, as on a cloned page, it loads an invisible image and raises an event.
en.guide:
# Script that detects a copy of your website

The file `site.js` is a script for the pages of your website `www.example.com`. If a browser loads a page that includes it from any other host, the script requests the invisible image `Honeytoken-URL`, which raises an event. On your own host it does nothing. That is what happens when someone copies your pages, including their scripts, to a server of their own to collect passwords from visitors.

## Placing the file

1. Upload the file to your web server, beside the other scripts, and include it in the pages that a copy would be made of, above all the login page: `<script src="/site.js"></script>`.
2. Rename it if your scripts follow another scheme, for example to `main.js`, and change the include to match.
3. If your pages are also served from other host names that you control, such as a test system, add those names to the list at the top of the script.
4. Record where you placed it in the notes of the scenario.

## Testing

Copy the login page with its scripts to another host, or open it from a local file, and load it in a browser. Within a minute, the scenario shows an incident. Close the incident after the test.

## Limits

- A copy that leaves out the scripts, or that removes this one, raises no event. Tools that copy pages as they are keep it.
- The script requests the image only when the host name differs. A test system or a preview that is not on the list raises events as well.
- The request shows the address of the page that loaded the script in its `Referer` header, if the browser sends it.

files.name: site.js

en.title: Scripts and notes of Windows administrators
en.summary: A script that maps a share, a recovery sheet for the local administrator and notes on the backup of group policies, with server names and passwords. Using them resolves the name of a DNS honeytoken.
en.guide:
# Scripts and notes of Windows administrators

Administrators of a Windows domain keep scripts and notes: a script that maps a share, a recovery sheet for the local administrator and notes on the backup of group policies. The files share the honeytokens of the story, so the same host name appears in every file that names the same service. Nothing stands behind the names: the accounts, tokens and passwords exist nowhere. You decide which files you place and where; one is enough, and they need not lie together.

## PowerShell script that maps a share

The file `Map-Share.ps1` connects the share `ops` on the server `Honeytoken-Domain-Share` with the account `CORP\svc-ops` and lists the ten newest files. The server name belongs to a DNS honeytoken: whoever runs the script, or connects to the share with the credentials, resolves the name, which raises an event. There is no server behind it, so the connection fails, and the account and password exist nowhere. The script only reads from the share and sends nothing from the computer on which it runs.

### Placing the file

1. Place the file where an intruder looks for scripts of administrators: on an administration server, on a file share of the IT department, in a folder with scripts in the profile of an account that exists only for this purpose.
2. Rename it if the place calls for another name, such as `Mount-Ops.ps1`. The extension `.ps1` must stay.
3. Do not place it where a scheduled task or a colleague runs it. Every run would resolve the name and raise an event.
4. Record where you placed it in the notes of the scenario.

### Testing

Run `nslookup Honeytoken-Domain-Share` on a computer with access to the internet; running the script in PowerShell has the same effect. Within a minute, the scenario shows an incident. Close the incident after the test.

## Recovery sheet for the local administrator

The file `Recovery.txt` is a break-glass sheet: it names the server `Honeytoken-Domain-Host`, the account `Administrator` and a random password. The server name belongs to a DNS honeytoken: whoever connects to the server over RDP or WinRM resolves the name, which raises an event. There is no server behind it, and the password exists nowhere.

### Placing the file

1. Print the sheet or save the file where emergency access is kept: in a folder of the IT department, in the documents of an account that exists only for this purpose, next to the documentation of the domain controllers.
2. Change `Contact` to a number or a team that exists.
3. Record where you placed it in the notes of the scenario.

### Testing

Resolve the name with `nslookup Honeytoken-Domain-Host` on a computer with access to the internet. Within a minute, the scenario shows an incident. Close the incident after the test.

## Notes on the backup of group policies

The file `GPO-Backup.txt` is a note of an administrator about the backups of the group policies. It names the share `\\Honeytoken-Domain-Share\GPOBackups$` and the account `CORP\svc-ops` with a random password. The server name belongs to a DNS honeytoken: whoever opens the share resolves the name, which raises an event. There is no server behind it, and the account and password exist nowhere.

### Placing the file

1. Place the file where an intruder looks for notes of administrators: on a domain controller or administration server, on a file share of the IT department, in the documents of an account that exists only for this purpose.
2. Change `Contact` to a team that exists, so that the note names someone who really works with group policies.
3. Record where you placed it in the notes of the scenario.

### Testing

Open `\\Honeytoken-Domain-Share\GPOBackups$` in the Windows Explorer of a computer with access to the internet, or resolve the name with `nslookup Honeytoken-Domain-Share`. Within a minute, the scenario shows an incident. Close the incident after the test.

## Limits

- Only a lookup that reaches the DNS role of Nyktus raises an event. A network without name resolution to the internet, or a resolver that answers from its cache, prevents it.
- The host names are random labels under the zone of your DNS role. An intruder who reads the files carefully can find them unusual.
- `Map-Share.ps1`: PowerShell stores the password in the script as text, as many scripts of administrators do. An intruder who runs the script on a computer with the execution policy `Restricted` is stopped before the lookup.
- `GPO-Backup.txt`: The note has no executable content. An event happens only when someone opens the share.

en.title: Linked image in a Word document
en.summary: A document of your own that links an invisible image. Word loads the image when someone opens the document and enables editing, also on the computer of an intruder who copied it.
en.guide:
# Linked image in a Word document

This deception has no file to download: you write the document yourself, so that it fits where you place it, and link this image in it:

```
Honeytoken-URL
```

The URL belongs to an image honeytoken. It always answers with an invisible image of one pixel. Word loads a linked image from its URL whenever it opens the document, and the request raises an event.

## Writing the document

Give the document content that an intruder wants to read where you place it, such as salary figures, a list of contacts for emergencies or the plan of a project. A document that holds nothing but an image stands out.

## Linking the image

1. Place the cursor at an inconspicuous spot, for example at the end of the document.
2. Press `Ctrl+F9`. Word inserts an empty field `{ }`.
3. Write between the braces:

   ```
   INCLUDEPICTURE "Honeytoken-URL" \d
   ```

   `\d` keeps Word from storing the image in the document, so that it loads it again with every opening.
4. Press `F9` to update the field, and save the document as `.docx`.

## Placing the document

Place it where an intruder searches for valuable data, such as a file share of the finance or personnel department, a document management system or a backup. Record where you placed it in the notes of the scenario.

## Testing

Open the document in Word on a computer with access to the internet and enable editing. Within a minute, the scenario shows an incident. Close the incident after the test.

## Limits

- Word opens documents from the internet and from some network shares in Protected View, which loads no images. Only "Enable Editing" sends the request.
- Mail gateways and previews can load the image without anyone opening the document. Do not send the document by mail.
- Other programs, such as LibreOffice or a viewer in the browser, may not load linked images.

en.title: Word document with a template on a remote host
en.summary: A document of your own that names a template on a remote host. Word resolves the host when someone opens the document, also on the computer of an intruder who copied it.
en.guide:
# Word document with a template on a remote host

This deception has no file to download: you write the document yourself, so that it fits where you place it, and attach a template to it that lies on this host:

```
Honeytoken-Domain
```

The name belongs to a DNS honeytoken. Word reads the attached template of a document when it opens it. If the template lies on a remote host, Word resolves the host name first, which raises an event. The lookup happens even when the connection to the host fails afterwards or the network blocks it.

## Writing the document

Give the document content that an intruder wants to read where you place it, such as a list of servers, a network plan or notes on a project. A document with a single empty page stands out. Save it as `.docx`.

## Attaching the template

1. Rename the file to `.zip` and unpack it.
2. In `word/settings.xml`, add this element directly before the element `<w:defaultTabStop`. Word is strict about the order of the elements in this file:

   ```
   <w:attachedTemplate r:id="rId1"/>
   ```

3. Create the file `word/_rels/settings.xml.rels` with this content, or, if it exists, add the `Relationship` to it:

   ```
   <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8" standalone="yes"?>
   <Relationships xmlns="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/package/2006/relationships">
     <Relationship Id="rId1" Type="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/relationships/attachedTemplate" Target="file:///\\Honeytoken-Domain\templates\normal.dotx" TargetMode="External"/>
   </Relationships>
   ```

4. Pack the files again, with `[Content_Types].xml` first, and rename the file back to `.docx`.

## Placing the document

Place it where an intruder searches for valuable data, such as a file share of the finance or personnel department, a document management system or a backup. Record where you placed it in the notes of the scenario.

## Testing

Open the document in Word on a computer with access to the internet and enable editing. Within a minute, the scenario shows an incident. Close the incident after the test.

## Limits

- Word opens documents from the internet and from some network shares in Protected View, which loads no remote template. Only "Enable Editing" starts the lookup.
- Only a lookup that reaches the DNS role of Nyktus raises an event. A network without name resolution to the internet, or a resolver that answers from its cache, prevents it.
- Other programs, such as LibreOffice or a viewer in the browser, do not load the template.
- The host name is a random label under the zone of your DNS role. An intruder who unpacks the document can find it unusual.
